report:
**Conclusion: yes.** Offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) in addition to, or instead of relying only on, conventional HIV-testing services causes more people to test, based on randomized-trial evidence synthesized in systematic reviews.

The strongest evidence is a 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials in general-population settings in sub-Saharan Africa. Compared with standard testing services, HIVST roughly doubled testing uptake (risk ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.69–2.58); the review rated this **moderate-certainty** evidence. Increased uptake was seen across facility distribution/use, community distribution, and secondary distribution to partners.  
https://hivevidence.org/examining-the-effects-of-hiv-self-testing-compared-to-standard-hiv-testing-services-in-the-general-population-a-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis/

An earlier systematic review/meta-analysis likewise found **moderate-quality evidence** that HIVST increases testing uptake. Its smaller evidence base also suggested more frequent testing, though certainty for that outcome was lower.  
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594

This conclusion is not merely about preference: the key evidence comes from trials comparing an HIVST offer with usual/standard services, so it supports a causal effect. WHO’s HIV-testing guidance reflects this evidence and recommends expanding self-testing within a differentiated mix of testing options.  
https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240096394

**Important qualification:** a self-test is a screening test; people with a reactive result need confirmatory testing and prompt linkage to HIV care. Programs should therefore pair expanded access with clear instructions and support for confirmation, prevention, and treatment.
